last_response.answer: Use one uniform welfare metric—e.g., expected remaining healthy life-years. last_response.answer: Yes. The Rawlsian comparison already represents the positions of both materially affected groups�the five elderly and the single child�over the same life-or-death horizon. Each action leaves one constituency dead and the other alive, so the worst-off in either scenario face identical deprivation of the basic good of life. Therefore the comparison remains complete but indeterminate; Rawlsian principles alone cannot rank the actions without an additional public tie-breaker (e.g. lottery).

last_response.answer: To satisfy Rawlsian validation the framework map must register that, under both actions, each person�s basic right to life is either fully preserved or fully lost. Because the least-advantaged fare equally (death) under each allocation, the comparison invokes the Original-Position Public-Rule test rather than the Difference Principle. Adding that public-rule grounde.g., "When maximal deprivation is identical, the parties behind the veil would endorse an impartial lottery to allocate the single life-saving resource"—resolves the mapping gap.

last_response.answer: Yes. The Rawlsian comparison already represents the positions of both materially affected groups�the five elderly and the single child�over the same life-or-death horizon. Each action leaves one constituency dead and the other alive, so the worst-off in either scenario face identical deprivation of the basic good of life. Therefore the comparison remains complete but indeterminate; Rawlsian principles alone cannot rank the actions without an additional public tie-breaker (e.g. lottery).
